verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, to the sons of Korah, a psalm.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, a psalm for the sons of Korah.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a heading, not part of the poem, and the KJV numbers it as verse 0 so that its own verse 1 is the Hebrew's verse 2. The Hebrew 'lamnatzeach' is a participle of a root meaning 'to excel, to be pre-eminent', so 'choirmaster' (or 'chief musician') is a tradition about the person who led the performance, not a certain definition. 'Livnei Korach' can mean 'for' or 'belonging to' the Korahite guild, Levitical singers; the KJV's 'for the sons of Korah' picks one preposition meaning among several. 'Mizmor' means a song sung to an instrument. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all read the psalm as composed for the Babylonian exile and its return; Malbim ties it to the days of Ezra and Nehemiah. Tell the actors the heading sets the voice: this is a choir, a public prayer, not a private murmur.

philological_notes.note: Piel participle with prefixed lamed, 'to the one who leads/excels'. The traditional translation 'choirmaster' is an inference from its use in the psalm headings, not a meaning given by the word itself.
A song sung with instrumental accompaniment; the heading word of many psalms.

verses.translation_literal: You were pleased, YHWH, [with] your land; you turned [the] captivity of Jacob.
verses.translation_dramatic: You were pleased with your land, O LORD. You turned the captivity of Jacob around, and brought them home.
verses.directors_commentary: The singers begin in the past tense, with a memory of a thing God has already done, and that is the ground for everything they will ask. 'Ratzita' is the language of acceptance, of a sacrifice that is received; God has accepted the land, and the land that was wrecked is now seen as his. The key idiom is 'shuv shevut', 'turn the captivity'. The KJV's 'brought back the captivity' is a fair guess, but the Hebrew idiom can mean 'reverse the fortunes' as well as 'return the exiles', and the bare verb is the same 'shuv', 'turn', that will return again and again through the psalm (verses 4, 5, 7, 9). The KJV hides this repetition behind 'brought back', 'turned thyself', 'turn us' and 'revive us again'. Rashi reads the whole verse as conditional, God's favor being granted on condition of what follows. Ibn Ezra places the event at the time of the Second Temple. The word is written 'shevut' but read 'shevit' (Ketiv and Qere); Radak says the two are the same.

philological_notes.note: The Qal of 'shuv', 'to turn', used with a causative sense, 'you turned [the captivity]'. Radak and Meiri explain this as equal to 'you made it return', 'hashivota', and some take it as 'you ended it'. The same root is repeated in verses 4, 5, 7 and 9.
'To be pleased with, to accept'; the term from sacrifice, where a gift is 'accepted'. Metzudat Zion derives it from 'ratzon', favor.

verses.translation_literal: You lifted [the] iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: You lifted the weight of your people's guilt and carried it away. You covered every one of their sins. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Two pictures of forgiveness, one after the other, and neither is the picture of erasing. 'Nasa' means 'to lift, to carry', as a man lifts a load and bears it off; the guilt is not abolished, it is taken up and carried by God. 'Kasah', 'to cover', is the second picture: sin is hidden from sight under a cloth. The KJV's 'forgiven' flattens the first image into a legal word, and the BBE's 'had forgiveness' does the same. Malbim sees a deliberate hint in the choice: a thing lifted still exists, a thing covered still lies underneath, and he reads the psalm's later prayers as asking that God remove them altogether; that is his own theology, not the plain sense. Note 'iniquity' (avon) and 'sin' (chatat): the first is the crooked deed and its guilt, the second the missing of a mark. 'Selah' is a liturgical mark of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or a musical interlude, and the KJV prints it as though it were a word; a director should treat it as a beat of silence.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'you lifted, you carried'. In the idiom 'nasa avon' it means to bear guilt away, i.e. to forgive; the underlying picture is of the burden being lifted.
'You covered', the Piel form: to hide from view. The pair 'lifted' and 'covered' occurs also in Psalm 32:1, to which Radak sends the reader.
A liturgical mark found in the Psalms; its meaning is unknown. It probably marked a pause, a musical interlude or a lifting of the voice.

verses.translation_literal: You gathered all your fury; you made [it] turn from the burning of your nose.
verses.translation_dramatic: You drew in all your fury, gathered it back to yourself. You turned away from the burning of your anger.
verses.directors_commentary: The anger of God is described as something that can be spread out and then gathered in again, like a cloak or a harvest. 'Asaf' means 'to gather, to take in', and Meiri compares it to putting a thing in storage so that it will never be brought out against them. The KJV's 'taken away' is wrong in nuance: the fury is not abolished, it is put away. 'Evrah' is the overflow of rage, the spilling over the bank, and 'charon af', 'the burning of the nose', is the Hebrew image for anger, the heat visible in the nostrils; the KJV's 'fierceness of thine anger' is an English abstraction for a physical picture. The verb 'heshivota' is causative: 'you made [the anger] turn'. Radak and Meiri say the object is the anger itself, as though 'you turned back your anger'; the KJV and ASV translate it as if God turned himself. Ibn Ezra and Radak also note that 'charon' is a form with an extra nun, like 'charut'.

philological_notes.note: 'To gather in, to withdraw'; Metzudat Zion compares the use in Judges 19:15, where no man 'gathers' the travelers into his house. The fury is taken in, not destroyed.
Hiphil, 'you made turn'. Radak and Meiri take the object as 'your anger'; Radak argues that if it were intransitive the text would say 'shavta', as in verse 2.
Fury, overflow, from the root 'to cross over'; the anger that crosses its limit.

verses.translation_literal: Turn us, God of our salvation, and break your vexation with us.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn us, God of our salvation, turn us back to you, and break your vexation with us.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now turns from what God did to what the people need, and the pivot is the same verb. 'Shuvenu' is 'turn us', and the ambiguity is real: turn us back to you, bring us back to the land, or turn back to us. Rashi hears it as 'turn, yourself, and bring us back'. The KJV's 'turn us' and the BBE's 'come back to us' pick opposite meanings. The actor should hear the repeated root: 'shavta' in verse 2, 'heshivota' in verse 4, now 'shuvenu'. 'Hafer' means 'to break, to make void', as one breaks a covenant or an oath; the KJV's 'cause to cease' softens a word of violence. 'Ka'as' is vexation, a provoked, irritated anger, not a burning fury, so the people are asking for the end of an irritation that has hung on for years (Radak: 'which had been with us for several years'). The prayer is no longer in the past tense, and the voice drops.

philological_notes.note: Qal imperative with 1cp suffix, 'turn us'. Rashi gives it the sense 'turn yourself and make us turn'. Metzudat David reads it as a request for a return from the last exile.
Hiphil imperative of 'parar', to break, to annul; used for breaking a covenant. Here it asks that God's anger be annulled.
Vexation, provocation; the anger of one who has been provoked, in contrast to 'charon', the burning of rage.

verses.translation_literal: Forever will you be angry with us? Will you draw out your anger to generation and generation?
verses.translation_dramatic: Will you be angry with us forever? Will you stretch out your anger, thin and long, down through one generation and the next?
verses.directors_commentary: Two questions, and the second sharpens the first. 'Le'olam' is 'for a vanishing point', as far as one can see; 'ledor vador' is the long chain of the generations, one after another. The KJV renders both with the same flat 'for ever' and 'to all generations', but the Hebrew sets the two against each other. 'Timshokh' is the verb for drawing out a cord or dragging a thing along, and so the anger is imagined as a rope pulled through the years. The verb 'te'enaf' is built on the same noun, 'af', 'nose', that has just appeared in 'the burning of your nose'; English can only say 'be angry' and 'anger', so keep them visibly related. Ibn Ezra says it is because the Babylonian exile lasted seventy years; Radak and Meiri say that the exile was long beyond reason. The voice is that of someone who has waited too long, tired, not shouting.

philological_notes.note: Verb 'to be angry', from the same word as 'af', 'nose, anger'; the word appears only of God's anger in the Hebrew Bible. Metzudat Zion links it to 'af' and 'chemah'.
'To draw, to drag, to prolong'; the image is of a cord or a line being pulled along.

verses.translation_literal: Will you not, you, turn [and] give us life, that your people may rejoice in you?
verses.translation_dramatic: Will you not turn again, and give us life, so that your people may rejoice in you?
verses.directors_commentary: The question is a rhetorical plea, a reasoned appeal: 'halo' means 'surely not?' and it expects the answer 'yes'. The pronoun 'attah', 'you', is emphatic and stands alone; the psalmist is pointing at God. The verbs 'tashuv techayenu' are two verbs in a row, 'you will turn, you will give us life', and the KJV's 'revive us again' makes the first an adverb. That is a legitimate reading but it drops the verb 'shuv', which is the thread of the whole psalm. YLT instead splits it as two clauses. For the ancient audience, life here is not an abstraction: Ibn Ezra says that in exile we were counted as the dead, and Rashi cites Ezekiel 37, the valley of dry bones. Joy is the purpose clause: 've'amkha yismechu vakh', 'your people will rejoice in you', which is the reverse of the grief of exile.

philological_notes.note: Piel, 'you will give us life, revive us'; Rashi connects it to Ezekiel 37, the revival of the dry bones, and Ibn Ezra reads exile as a kind of death.
Interrogative 'ha' with 'lo', 'not': a question that expects a yes. The sense is 'surely you will'.

verses.translation_literal: Make us see, YHWH, your covenant loyalty, and your salvation give to us.
verses.translation_dramatic: Show us, LORD, show us your faithful love, and put your deliverance into our hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a request spoken by people who have just been told, in the verses before, that they live under anger. The Hebrew is not the gentle 'shew us' of the KJV: har'enu is a causative, 'make us see', the verb of sight set on the LORD as the one who must act so that the people may look. They are asking for something visible, not a feeling. Then the second half turns on the verb 'give' (titten), which will come back in verse 13 when the land gives its produce, so the plea here and the promise there are tied by one word.

The KJV 'mercy' for chesed is a weak choice: chesed is loyalty inside a covenant, the obligation a party keeps because of the bond, and the people are appealing to the bond, not to pity. 'Grant' for 'give' blurs the repetition that the Hebrew keeps, and YLT, reading the imperfect as a plain statement ('Thou dost give'), turns a plea into a report. Play it as a plea, with the pause that Hebrew accents leave after 'your loyalty'. Note also the odd vowel on 'your salvation', which the medieval commentators noticed.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, the faithfulness one owes within a bond. Radak reads it as the kindness God does toward sinners without repaying them as their wrongs deserve, which is why the people can ask for it even when their guilt is heavy.
The segol under the yod is unusual (the usual form is yish'akha), which is why Radak and Meiri remark on it; Meiri compares the pointing in Psalm 38. The sense is not affected: 'and your salvation'.

verses.translation_literal: I will hear what the God YHWH will speak, for he speaks peace to his people and to his faithful ones, and let them not turn to folly.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will listen. I will hear what God, the LORD, will say, for he speaks peace to his people, to his faithful ones. Only let them never turn back to folly.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice changes. Until now the choir has spoken for the community; here a single speaker, 'I', stands still and waits for an answer, as a prophet or a Levitical watchman might. Ibn Ezra explicitly calls it prophecy, comparing it to Habakkuk standing on his watch. The Hebrew 'eshme'ah' is a cohortative, 'let me hear', and the KJV's 'I will hear' leaves out the eagerness. What he expects to hear is 'shalom', not just the absence of war but wholeness, the state of lacking nothing. The KJV's 'saints' for 'chasidav' is a Christian-era coinage; the word means 'those loyal to the covenant', the ones who practice chesed. The final clause is a jussive wish: 've'al yashuvu lechislah', 'and let them not turn to folly'. YLT reads it as a statement; the KJV, ASV and BBE read it as a wish. 'Kislah' is stupidity as moral failing (Rashi: 'sheṭut', folly, to sin before him). The repeated verb 'shuv' returns here, now a warning.

philological_notes.note: 'His faithful ones', from the same root as 'chesed': those who keep covenant loyalty. The KJV 'saints' carries later associations.
Folly, from the same root as 'kesil', fool. Rashi glosses it as foolishness, which is to sin before God; Meiri reads it as an infinitive 'to act foolishly'.
Wholeness, completeness; Malbim ties it to 'kiyyum', continued existence.

verses.translation_literal: Surely near to those who fear him [is] his salvation, for glory to dwell in our land.
verses.translation_dramatic: His salvation is near, near to those who fear him, so that his glory may settle and dwell in our land.
verses.directors_commentary: The answer arrives and it is a promise with a condition built in: salvation is near to those who fear him. 'Ach' opens the line as 'surely, only', a word that both assures and limits (YLT: 'Only'), so the KJV's flat 'Surely' loses the narrowing. Radak says the redemption depends on repentance. 'Yirei'av', 'those fearing him', is reverence, not terror. The goal is 'lishkon kavod', 'for glory to dwell', and the verb 'shakhan' is the tent-dwelling verb that gives us 'shekhinah', the presence that settles. The land is to become a place where God's weight, 'kavod', lives, and this sets up the Temple background. Ibn Ezra and Meiri add that the glory did not dwell in the Second Temple, and Meiri cites the Talmudic list of what was missing there; Malbim reads the verse as steering between pure grace and pure merit. Whatever the reading, the actor should play 'near' twice: close enough to touch.

philological_notes.note: 'To dwell, to settle', the verb used of the tabernacle and the presence; 'kavod' is God's weight, his glory. Radak links it to the Temple, citing 'and I will dwell among the children of Israel'.
'Surely, only'; asserts and restricts at once.

verses.translation_literal: Covenant loyalty and faithfulness have met; righteousness and peace have kissed.
verses.translation_dramatic: Covenant love and faithfulness have met on the road. Righteousness and peace have kissed.
verses.directors_commentary: Four abstract nouns become four persons, two pairs, and the stage direction is physical: they meet, they kiss. The KJV says 'mercy and truth are met together' and 'kissed each other', which is fair, but 'truth' for 'emet' loses the idea of reliability: 'emet' is firmness, the thing that holds when you lean on it. 'Chesed' and 'emet' are the two words used together for God's reliability in the covenant. The verb 'nifgashu' is for travelers who meet on a road; the greeting of friends at a crossing. Malbim's picture is the most vivid: faithfulness climbs up from the earth, and covenant loyalty comes down from heaven, and they meet halfway. 'Nashaku' is the real kiss of greeting, of kin; Radak says 'brothers and friends'. Do not let the actors treat this as a poem about concepts: it is a reunion at a crossroads, and the next verse says where each came from.

philological_notes.note: 'They met', the verb for people encountering each other on a road; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'pegi'ah', meeting.
'They kissed', the kiss of greeting between kin and friends; Radak glosses it as 'brothers and friends'.

verses.translation_literal: Faithfulness from [the] earth sprouts, and righteousness from heaven looks down.
verses.translation_dramatic: Faithfulness springs up out of the earth like new green, and righteousness leans down out of heaven to look.
verses.directors_commentary: The picture of the previous verse is now given its two directions, earth and sky. 'Tzamach' is the verb for plants sprouting: the KJV's 'shall spring out of the earth' is good, and the BBE's 'like a plant' makes the picture explicit. Faithfulness here grows from below like a crop, in a land that has been waiting for rain; from above 'tzedek' (righteousness, what is right) 'nishkaf', 'leans out, looks down', a word used of someone looking through a window or over a wall. The tenses are an issue: the KJV says 'shall', the ASV says 'hath looked down'; the Hebrew has an imperfect and a perfect, and the translations differ on whether this is promise or description. Rashi and Radak both explain it as a bargain: when people on earth speak truth and do justice, heaven looks down on them with righteousness, since decrees from above follow deeds below. Metzudat David and Malbim agree that the earth's part must come first, as with a field that must be plowed before the rain helps. The agricultural frame also prepares verse 13 of the Hebrew's rain and harvest.

philological_notes.note: 'It sprouts', the verb for plants growing from the ground; used here of faithfulness rising from the earth.
'It looks down, it peers out'; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'histakkelut', looking. It is used of someone looking out from a high place.

verses.translation_literal: Also YHWH will give the good, and our land will give its produce.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD himself will give what is good; and our land, in answer, will give back its harvest.
verses.directors_commentary:
This closes the picture of verses 11 and 12: truth rising from the ground, righteousness leaning down from the sky, and now the two movements meet in an ordinary field. The audience was farmers, and for them the sentence is about rain and grain. The old commentators say so plainly: Radak and Ibn Ezra identify 'the good' with the rain, and Rashi and Radak quote Deuteronomy 28:12, 'The LORD will open to you his good treasure, the heavens, to give rain to your land in its season.'

Two things are worth noting against the KJV. It renders the first word, gam, as 'Yea', which makes it an emphatic opening; the Hebrew means 'also' or 'moreover', a word that adds this gift to what has already been promised. And 'that which is good' adds words: the Hebrew has only ha-tov, 'the good', with the article, as a known thing. The verb 'give' stands in both halves, the LORD giving from above and the land giving from below: a parallel, with the same order, subject, verb and object, in each half, and the repetition itself carries the point. The verb of the first half also recalls verse 8, where the people asked the LORD to give his salvation. 'Her increase' in the KJV is faithful to the feminine suffix on yevulah, as 'land' is feminine in Hebrew, but modern English says 'its'.

philological_notes.note: 'Also, moreover'. It adds this gift to what has gone before; Metzudat David reads it as 'beyond the reward for their deeds'. KJV 'Yea' makes it an emphatic opener.
The produce of the land, what the ground brings forth. Metzudat Zion glosses it as its crop and its fruit. The suffix is feminine because 'land' (erets) is feminine.

verses.translation_literal: Righteousness before him will walk, and will set [it] to the way of his footsteps.
verses.translation_dramatic: Righteousness walks ahead of him, a herald going before the King. And where his feet will fall, she lays down the road.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a procession. In the ancient Near East a king or a god did not travel alone: a herald or forerunner went ahead to clear the road and announce his coming. Here that role is given to Righteousness (tzedek), personified, just as in vv. 11-12 Faithfulness, Righteousness and Peace meet and kiss. The divine presence arrives, and what precedes him is not an army but justice.

The second half is hard, and the KJV smooths it: 'and shall set us in the way of his steps'. The word 'us' is not in the Hebrew (Webster rightly brackets it). Literally, the verb 'sets' has no stated object, and the line says 'to the way of his footsteps'. Either Righteousness makes his footsteps into a path to follow, or it makes ready the road where he will step, or he sets Righteousness in his own way. Rashi takes the last view, with God setting righteousness in the ways in which he leads his children; Malbim has the Good following behind Righteousness as a guide; Radak and Metzudat David read it as a doubling for emphasis. 'Pe'amav' (his footsteps) is a plural of the step itself, so the image has rhythm: steps, one after another.

philological_notes.note: 'Righteousness', here a personified forerunner. Ibn Ezra offers that the word stands for 'a man of righteousness' with 'ish' omitted.
'And will set / make': no object is given, and the subject can be Righteousness or YHWH; the ambiguity is the reason translations diverge.
'His footsteps', or 'his steps': Metzudat Zion glosses it 'his steps', comparing a verse in Psalm 119. The word also means 'time, occasion' elsewhere.
